content: Tuberculous meningitis is a severe manifestation of tuberculosis that affects the meninges, the protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord. This condition is associated with high mortality rates and significant disability among survivors. Corticosteroids have been used as an adjunctive therapy alongside antituberculous drugs to manage this condition, but their efficacy and role remain a topic of debate. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of corticosteroids, when used in combination with antituberculous treatment, on reducing mortality and severe disability in patients with tuberculous meningitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and Current Controlled Trials, up to March 18, 2016. Researchers and organizations in the field were also contacted, and reference lists were reviewed for additional studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials that compared corticosteroid therapy combined with antituberculous treatment to antituberculous treatment alone in patients with clinically diagnosed tuberculous meningitis. The primary outcomes assessed were death and disability. Data from the included trials were independently evaluated for methodological quality, and statistical analyses were performed using risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A fixed-effect model was employed, and an intention-to-treat analysis was conducted, assuming favorable outcomes for participants lost to follow-up. Sensitivity analyses were performed to account for the impact of missing data. Nine trials, encompassing a total of 1,337 participants, met the inclusion criteria. Among these participants, 469 deaths were reported. The results demonstrated that corticosteroids reduced mortality by nearly 25% during follow-up periods ranging from three to 18 months (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.87; high-quality evidence). However, corticosteroids appeared to have little or no effect on the incidence of disabling neurological deficits among survivors (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.20; low-quality evidence). Adverse events, such as gastrointestinal bleeding, invasive bacterial infections, hyperglycemia, and liver dysfunction, were reported at similar rates in both the corticosteroid and control groups. One trial followed participants for five years and found that the mortality-reducing effect of corticosteroids was no longer evident at this extended time point (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.12; moderate-quality evidence). Additionally, no significant difference in disabling neurological deficits was observed at this time (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.69; low-quality evidence). A single trial included participants who were HIV-positive. In this subgroup, stratified analysis revealed no significant differences in outcomes compared to HIV-negative participants. The risk ratio for death in HIV-positive individuals was 0.90 (95% CI 0.67 to 1.20), and for disability, it was 1.23 (95% CI 0.08 to 19.07), though the small sample size limited the reliability of these findings. In conclusion, corticosteroids appear to reduce short-term mortality in patients with tuberculous meningitis. However, they may have little or no effect on the incidence of disabling neurological deficits among survivors, though this outcome is less common than death. The confidence interval for the relative effect on disability includes the possibility of harm, but this potential harm is likely to be minor when weighed against the reduction in mortality. The evidence regarding the benefits of corticosteroids in HIV-positive individuals is limited due to the small number of participants in this subgroup, and further research is needed to clarify their efficacy in this population.
